_link.title: I can describe the capacity and duration of sensory memory

toLevel2.stem: What is the capacity of sensory memory?

options.text: Unlimited
options.feedback: Correct. Sensory memory has an unlimited capacity, briefly holding all sensory information that is received.

options.text: Seven plus or minus two items
options.feedback: Incorrect. The capacity of seven plus or minus two items describes short-term memory, not sensory memory.

options.text: Three to four items
options.feedback: Incorrect. This does not accurately describe the capacity of sensory memory, which is unlimited.

options.text: One item at a time
options.feedback: Incorrect. Sensory memory can hold far more than one item; its capacity is unlimited.

toLevel2.stem: What is the approximate duration of iconic (visual) sensory memory?

options.text: 0.2 to 0.4 seconds
options.feedback: Correct. Iconic memory, the visual component of sensory memory, lasts approximately 0.2 to 0.4 seconds.

options.text: 3 to 4 seconds
options.feedback: Incorrect. A duration of 3 to 4 seconds describes echoic (auditory) sensory memory, not iconic memory.

options.text: 18 to 20 seconds
options.feedback: Incorrect. A duration of 18 to 20 seconds is associated with short-term memory without rehearsal, not sensory memory.

options.text: 30 to 60 seconds
options.feedback: Incorrect. This duration far exceeds that of sensory memory, which lasts only fractions of a second for visual information.

toLevel2.stem: What is the approximate duration of echoic (auditory) sensory memory?

options.text: 3 to 4 seconds
options.feedback: Correct. Echoic memory, the auditory component of sensory memory, lasts approximately 3 to 4 seconds.

options.text: 0.2 to 0.4 seconds
options.feedback: Incorrect. A duration of 0.2 to 0.4 seconds describes iconic (visual) sensory memory, not echoic memory.

options.text: 18 to 20 seconds
options.feedback: Incorrect. This duration is associated with short-term memory, not echoic sensory memory.

options.text: Up to a lifetime
options.feedback: Incorrect. A lifetime duration describes long-term memory, not sensory memory.

toLevel2.stem: Which term refers to the visual component of sensory memory?

options.text: Iconic memory
options.feedback: Correct. Iconic memory is the term for the visual component of sensory memory.

options.text: Echoic memory
options.feedback: Incorrect. Echoic memory refers to the auditory component of sensory memory, not the visual component.

options.text: Episodic memory
options.feedback: Incorrect. Episodic memory is a type of explicit long-term memory for personal experiences, not a sensory memory component.

options.text: Semantic memory
options.feedback: Incorrect. Semantic memory is a type of explicit long-term memory for factual knowledge, not a sensory memory component.

toLevel2.stem: The overall duration of sensory memory ranges from approximately which of the following?

options.text: 0.2 to 4 seconds
options.feedback: Correct. Sensory memory duration ranges from approximately 0.2 seconds (iconic) to 4 seconds (echoic), depending on the sensory modality.

options.text: 5 to 20 seconds
options.feedback: Incorrect. This range is more consistent with short-term memory duration, not sensory memory.

options.text: 1 to 10 minutes
options.feedback: Incorrect. Sensory memory lasts only seconds at most, not minutes.

options.text: 20 to 30 seconds
options.feedback: Incorrect. This range describes the typical duration of short-term memory, not sensory memory.

toLevel2.stem: Sensory memory has an unlimited capacity.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Correct. Sensory memory can briefly hold all incoming sensory information, giving it an unlimited capacity.

options.text: False
options.feedback: Incorrect. Sensory memory does have an unlimited capacity; it is short-term memory that has a limited capacity.

toLevel2.stem: Iconic memory lasts longer than echoic memory.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Incorrect. Iconic memory lasts approximately 0.2 to 0.4 seconds, which is shorter than echoic memory at approximately 3 to 4 seconds.

options.text: False
options.feedback: Correct. Echoic memory (3–4 seconds) lasts considerably longer than iconic memory (0.2–0.4 seconds).

toLevel2.stem: Sensory memory has an {{blank:1}} capacity but an extremely {{blank:2}} duration.
The visual component of sensory memory is called {{blank:1}} memory, while the auditory component is called {{blank:2}} memory.
Iconic memory lasts approximately {{blank:1}} seconds, while echoic memory lasts approximately {{blank:2}} seconds.

toLevel3.stem: Why does information in sensory memory fade so quickly if it is not attended to?

options.text: Because sensory memory has an extremely brief duration and unattended information is lost before further processing
options.feedback: Correct. The brief duration of sensory memory (0.2–4 seconds) means that without attention, information decays before it can be transferred to short-term memory.

options.text: Because sensory memory has a very limited capacity and new information displaces old information
options.feedback: Incorrect. Sensory memory has unlimited capacity; loss of information is due to its brief duration, not displacement from limited capacity.

options.text: Because sensory memory requires rehearsal to maintain information for any period of time
options.feedback: Incorrect. Rehearsal is a strategy for maintaining information in short-term memory, not sensory memory.

options.text: Because sensory memory stores information in long-term memory before it can be consciously perceived
options.feedback: Incorrect. Information must pass through sensory memory and short-term memory before reaching long-term memory; it does not bypass conscious processing.

toLevel3.stem: Which of the following best explains why echoic memory lasts longer than iconic memory?

options.text: Auditory information requires a longer trace to process speech and sequential sounds
options.feedback: Correct. Echoic memory persists longer (3–4 seconds) because auditory information, such as speech, unfolds over time and requires a longer trace to be meaningfully processed.

options.text: Visual information is more complex and therefore requires a shorter storage duration
options.feedback: Incorrect. The shorter duration of iconic memory is not due to visual complexity but relates to the different processing demands of visual versus auditory information.

options.text: Echoic memory has a larger capacity than iconic memory, allowing it to store information longer
options.feedback: Incorrect. Both iconic and echoic memory have unlimited capacity; the difference in duration is related to processing demands, not capacity.

options.text: Iconic memory is stored in long-term memory more quickly than echoic memory
options.feedback: Incorrect. Neither iconic nor echoic memory is stored directly in long-term memory; both must first be attended to and transferred to short-term memory.

toLevel3.stem: A student glances at a page of notes and then looks away. She can briefly 'see' the page in her mind but the image fades almost immediately. Which feature of sensory memory does this illustrate?

options.text: The extremely brief duration of iconic sensory memory
options.feedback: Correct. The brief visual trace that fades within fractions of a second is characteristic of iconic memory, which lasts approximately 0.2 to 0.4 seconds.

options.text: The limited capacity of iconic sensory memory
options.feedback: Incorrect. Sensory memory has unlimited capacity; the fading is due to its brief duration, not limited capacity.

options.text: The long duration of echoic sensory memory
options.feedback: Incorrect. This example involves visual information (iconic memory), not auditory information (echoic memory).

options.text: The transfer of information from long-term memory to sensory memory
options.feedback: Incorrect. Information flows from sensory memory to short-term memory, not from long-term memory back to sensory memory.

toLevel3.stem: What is the relationship between attention and sensory memory in the Atkinson-Shiffrin model?

options.text: Attention selects which information in sensory memory is transferred to short-term memory
options.feedback: Correct. In the Atkinson-Shiffrin model, attention acts as a filter that determines which information from sensory memory is selected for further processing in short-term memory.

options.text: Attention increases the capacity of sensory memory to hold more information simultaneously
options.feedback: Incorrect. Sensory memory already has unlimited capacity; attention does not change this but instead determines what is transferred onward.

options.text: Attention extends the duration of sensory memory from seconds to several minutes
options.feedback: Incorrect. Attention does not extend sensory memory duration; rather, it selects information for transfer to short-term memory before sensory memory fades.

options.text: Attention transfers information directly from sensory memory into long-term memory storage
options.feedback: Incorrect. In the Atkinson-Shiffrin model, attended information from sensory memory goes to short-term memory first, not directly to long-term memory.

toLevel3.stem: A teacher claps their hands loudly. Students can still 'hear' the clap for a few seconds after the sound has stopped. Which type of sensory memory is responsible?

options.text: Echoic memory
options.feedback: Correct. The brief persistence of an auditory trace after the sound has ended is characteristic of echoic memory, which lasts approximately 3 to 4 seconds.

options.text: Iconic memory
options.feedback: Incorrect. Iconic memory is the visual component of sensory memory, not the auditory component.

options.text: Short-term memory
options.feedback: Incorrect. The immediate auditory trace before conscious processing is a function of echoic sensory memory, not short-term memory.

options.text: Procedural memory
options.feedback: Incorrect. Procedural memory involves learned motor skills stored in long-term memory, not brief sensory traces.

toLevel3.stem: Why is it accurate to say that sensory memory has unlimited capacity but most information is still lost?

options.text: Because its extremely brief duration means unattended information decays before it can be processed further
options.feedback: Correct. Although sensory memory can hold all incoming sensory information, its very short duration (0.2–4 seconds) means that any information not selected by attention will decay rapidly.

options.text: Because sensory memory actively deletes information that is not immediately relevant to survival
options.feedback: Incorrect. Information in sensory memory fades passively due to its brief duration, not through an active deletion process.

options.text: Because sensory memory transfers all information to short-term memory where it is then lost
options.feedback: Incorrect. Only attended information is transferred to short-term memory; unattended information is lost at the sensory memory stage.

options.text: Because the unlimited capacity causes interference that prevents any information from being retained
options.feedback: Incorrect. The loss is due to the brief duration of sensory memory, not interference from its unlimited capacity.

toLevel3.stem: In the Atkinson-Shiffrin model, attention determines which information in sensory memory is transferred to short-term memory.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Correct. Attention acts as a selective mechanism that determines which sensory information is processed further into short-term memory.

options.text: False
options.feedback: Incorrect. Attention does play this selective role in the Atkinson-Shiffrin model, filtering sensory information for transfer to short-term memory.

toLevel3.stem: Information in sensory memory that is not {{blank:1}} will be lost due to the store's extremely brief {{blank:2}}.
Echoic memory lasts longer than iconic memory because {{blank:1}} information unfolds over time and requires a longer {{blank:2}} for processing.
Despite its {{blank:1}} capacity, sensory memory loses most information because its {{blank:2}} is only 0.2 to 4 seconds.

toLevel4.stem: During a busy lecture, Priya hears the lecturer mention an important date but does not write it down. A few seconds later, she realises she should note it and can still recall the sound of the lecturer's voice saying the date. Which sensory memory store enabled this?

options.text: Echoic memory, which retained the auditory trace for several seconds
options.feedback: Correct. Echoic memory retains auditory information for approximately 3 to 4 seconds, allowing Priya to access the sound trace shortly after it occurred.

options.text: Iconic memory, which retained the visual trace of the lecturer speaking
options.feedback: Incorrect. Iconic memory stores visual information, not auditory information. The auditory trace Priya recalled is stored in echoic memory.

options.text: Short-term memory, which stored the date through rehearsal
options.feedback: Incorrect. Priya did not actively rehearse the information; she accessed the raw auditory trace still available in echoic sensory memory.

options.text: Long-term memory, which encoded the date automatically during the lecture
options.feedback: Incorrect. The date was not encoded into long-term memory; Priya was accessing a brief sensory trace that had not yet been processed further.

toLevel4.stem: Marcus briefly sees a car number plate as a vehicle speeds past but cannot recall all the characters a moment later. Which characteristic of sensory memory best explains this?

options.text: The brief duration of iconic memory caused the visual trace to fade before all characters could be processed
options.feedback: Correct. Iconic memory lasts only 0.2 to 0.4 seconds, so the visual trace of the number plate faded before Marcus could attend to and process all the characters.

options.text: The limited capacity of iconic memory prevented all the characters from being stored simultaneously
options.feedback: Incorrect. Iconic memory has unlimited capacity; the loss is due to its brief duration, not limited capacity.

options.text: The long duration of echoic memory interfered with the visual information being processed
options.feedback: Incorrect. Echoic memory processes auditory information and does not interfere with visual iconic memory.

options.text: Short-term memory displaced the number plate information before it could be encoded
options.feedback: Incorrect. The information was lost at the sensory memory stage due to its brief duration, before it reached short-term memory.

toLevel4.stem: A researcher briefly flashes twelve letters on a screen for 50 milliseconds. Participants report seeing all the letters but can only recall about four. Sperling's partial report technique then shows they actually stored more. What does this demonstrate about sensory memory?

options.text: Sensory memory has a large capacity but the information decays before it can all be reported
options.feedback: Correct. Sperling's research demonstrated that sensory memory briefly holds more information than can be reported, because the iconic trace fades during the time it takes to recall items.

options.text: Sensory memory has a capacity of only four items at any given time
options.feedback: Incorrect. The four-item recall limit reflects the decay of the iconic trace during reporting, not the actual capacity of sensory memory, which is much larger.

options.text: Sensory memory transfers all twelve letters into long-term memory simultaneously
options.feedback: Incorrect. Sensory memory does not transfer information directly to long-term memory; only attended items move to short-term memory.

options.text: Sensory memory lasts long enough for all items to be reported without any information loss
options.feedback: Incorrect. The inability to report all items demonstrates that sensory memory is too brief for complete recall, which is why the partial report technique was needed.

toLevel4.stem: While walking through a crowded market, Zara hears someone call her name from behind. Even though she was not paying attention, she can still identify the voice a moment later. Which explanation best accounts for this?

options.text: Echoic memory retained the auditory information long enough for Zara to direct her attention to it
options.feedback: Correct. Echoic memory lasts 3 to 4 seconds, providing a brief window during which Zara could redirect her attention to the auditory trace and identify the voice.

options.text: Iconic memory stored a visual trace of the person calling her name from behind
options.feedback: Incorrect. Iconic memory stores visual information, and Zara heard the voice from behind without seeing the person.

options.text: Long-term memory enabled automatic recognition of the voice without any sensory processing
options.feedback: Incorrect. While voice recognition involves long-term memory, the initial retention of the sound relied on echoic sensory memory.

options.text: Short-term memory rehearsed the sound before Zara became aware of hearing it
options.feedback: Incorrect. Short-term memory requires attention and conscious processing; the initial sound retention occurred in echoic sensory memory before attention was directed to it.

toLevel4.stem: A sports coach shows players a brief video clip of an opponent's play formation. The image disappears after half a second. Players who were attending to the screen recall more details than those who were distracted. How does sensory memory explain this difference?

options.text: Attending players transferred more information from iconic memory to short-term memory before the trace decayed
options.feedback: Correct. Both groups had the same iconic memory trace, but attending players used attention to transfer more information to short-term memory before the brief iconic trace (0.2–0.4 seconds) faded.

options.text: Attending players had a larger iconic memory capacity than distracted players
options.feedback: Incorrect. Iconic memory capacity is unlimited for all individuals; the difference is in how much was transferred through attention, not in capacity.

options.text: Distracted players had no iconic memory trace of the video clip at all
options.feedback: Incorrect. All players would have had an iconic memory trace; the difference is that distracted players did not attend to it before it decayed.

options.text: Attending players encoded the information directly into long-term memory from sensory memory
options.feedback: Incorrect. In the Atkinson-Shiffrin model, information must pass through short-term memory before reaching long-term memory; it cannot go directly from sensory to long-term memory.

toLevel4.stem: During a phone conversation, Elijah asks his friend to repeat a number. His friend says, 'I just told you!' Elijah then realises he can still 'hear' the number in his mind. Which feature of sensory memory allowed this?

options.text: The 3 to 4 second duration of echoic memory preserved the auditory trace
options.feedback: Correct. Echoic memory retains auditory information for approximately 3 to 4 seconds, giving Elijah a brief window to access the number he initially did not attend to.

options.text: The 0.2 to 0.4 second duration of iconic memory preserved a visual trace
options.feedback: Incorrect. The information was auditory (heard during a phone call), so it would be stored in echoic memory, not iconic memory.

options.text: The unlimited duration of long-term memory allowed permanent storage of the number
options.feedback: Incorrect. Elijah nearly lost the number, indicating it was in brief sensory storage, not permanent long-term memory.

options.text: The limited capacity of short-term memory prevented the number from being encoded
options.feedback: Incorrect. The issue was not short-term memory capacity but rather that Elijah initially failed to attend to the auditory trace in echoic memory.

toLevel4.stem: A student is studying in a noisy café and does not notice a friend greeting them. Five seconds later, the student has no trace of the greeting. Which aspect of sensory memory explains this?

options.text: The echoic memory trace lasted only 3 to 4 seconds and decayed before attention was directed to it
options.feedback: Correct. Echoic memory lasts approximately 3 to 4 seconds. After 5 seconds, the auditory trace would have completely decayed without attention.

options.text: The iconic memory trace of the greeting was overwritten by new visual information
options.feedback: Incorrect. A verbal greeting is auditory information stored in echoic memory, not visual information in iconic memory.

options.text: The student's long-term memory actively suppressed the unimportant information
options.feedback: Incorrect. The information was lost due to the natural decay of the echoic memory trace, not active suppression by long-term memory.

options.text: Sensory memory has limited capacity and the café noise prevented the greeting from being stored
options.feedback: Incorrect. Sensory memory has unlimited capacity and would have briefly stored the greeting; the loss occurred because the trace decayed before attention was directed to it.

toLevel4.stem: When Priya heard a number mentioned during a lecture and recalled it seconds later without rehearsal, she was accessing her {{blank:1}} memory, which lasts approximately {{blank:2}} seconds.
Marcus could not recall all the characters on a number plate because the {{blank:1}} memory trace decayed within {{blank:2}} seconds before he could attend to every character.
Sperling's research demonstrated that sensory memory has a {{blank:1}} capacity, but information is lost rapidly because of its extremely brief {{blank:2}}.

toLevel5.stem: Sperling's partial report technique showed that participants could recall any cued row of letters if cued immediately, but performance declined as the cue was delayed. What does this pattern of results reveal about sensory memory?

options.text: Sensory memory initially holds more information than can be reported, but the trace decays rapidly over time
options.feedback: Correct. The declining performance with delayed cues demonstrates that the iconic memory trace fades rapidly; immediate cues capture information before decay, confirming a large but brief store.

options.text: Sensory memory holds only the cued row of information and discards the rest immediately
options.feedback: Incorrect. The ability to recall any cued row shows that all rows were initially stored; the store does not selectively hold only cued information.

options.text: Sensory memory has a limited capacity that only allows one row to be stored at a time
options.feedback: Incorrect. Participants could recall any row when cued immediately, indicating all rows were stored simultaneously, demonstrating large capacity.

options.text: Sensory memory duration increases when participants are given more time to prepare for the cue
options.feedback: Incorrect. The duration of sensory memory is fixed; preparation time does not extend the iconic trace.

toLevel5.stem: A researcher argues that the distinction between iconic and echoic memory is unnecessary because both are simply forms of sensory memory. Which evidence would most strongly challenge this argument?

options.text: The two stores have markedly different durations, suggesting distinct processing mechanisms for different modalities
options.feedback: Correct. Iconic memory (0.2–0.4 s) and echoic memory (3–4 s) have substantially different durations, which suggests they involve different processing mechanisms rather than being identical stores.

options.text: Both stores have unlimited capacity, which confirms they are identical in function
options.feedback: Incorrect. Shared unlimited capacity does not demonstrate they are identical; the significant difference in duration indicates distinct functional properties.

options.text: Both stores are located within the same region of the cerebral cortex
options.feedback: Incorrect. Visual and auditory processing occur in different cortical regions, which would actually support the distinction rather than challenge the argument.

options.text: Both stores feed information into short-term memory through the same attentional process
options.feedback: Incorrect. The shared attentional mechanism for transfer does not eliminate the need to distinguish between the two stores based on their differing properties.

toLevel5.stem: A textbook claims that sensory memory is the 'least important' memory store because information is lost so quickly. Which evaluation of this claim is most justified?

options.text: The claim underestimates the critical role sensory memory plays in holding information long enough for attention to select what is relevant
options.feedback: Correct. Without sensory memory, there would be no brief buffer for incoming information, and attention would have nothing to select from. Sensory memory is essential as the first stage of information processing.

options.text: The claim is accurate because any memory store with such a short duration cannot serve a meaningful cognitive function
options.feedback: Incorrect. Despite its brief duration, sensory memory serves the essential function of holding all incoming information so that attention can select what to process further.

options.text: The claim is accurate because sensory memory does not interact with any other component of the memory system
options.feedback: Incorrect. Sensory memory directly feeds into short-term memory through the mechanism of attention, making it a crucial first step in the memory system.

options.text: The claim is valid because long-term memory can receive information directly without needing sensory memory
options.feedback: Incorrect. In the Atkinson-Shiffrin model, sensory memory is the entry point for information into the memory system; information cannot bypass it to reach long-term memory.

toLevel5.stem: A student argues that sensory memory must have limited capacity because people cannot recall everything they see or hear. Which response best evaluates this reasoning?

options.text: The reasoning confuses capacity with duration; sensory memory holds all information briefly but loses it due to rapid decay, not limited capacity
options.feedback: Correct. Sperling's research demonstrated that sensory memory holds more than can be reported. The limitation is the brief duration causing rapid decay, not a capacity restriction.

options.text: The reasoning is correct because Sperling's research confirmed that only a few items can enter sensory memory
options.feedback: Incorrect. Sperling's partial report technique demonstrated the opposite: sensory memory holds far more information than people can report in the time before it decays.

options.text: The reasoning is correct because unlimited capacity would mean nothing could ever be forgotten at this stage
options.feedback: Incorrect. Information can be forgotten from a store with unlimited capacity if the store has a very brief duration, which is exactly how sensory memory operates.

options.text: The reasoning is valid because sensory memory capacity varies depending on intelligence and cognitive ability
options.feedback: Incorrect. Sensory memory capacity is considered unlimited across individuals; the difference in recall relates to attention and the brief duration of the store.

toLevel5.stem: A cognitive psychologist finds that participants in a noisy environment show reduced recall from brief visual displays compared to participants in a quiet environment. Assuming sensory memory capacity is unaffected, which explanation is most consistent with current understanding?

options.text: Noise diverted attentional resources, reducing the amount of information transferred from iconic memory to short-term memory before the trace decayed
options.feedback: Correct. If iconic memory capacity is unaffected, the reduced recall is best explained by noise diverting attention, which left less attentional capacity to select and transfer visual information before the iconic trace faded.

options.text: Noise directly shortened the duration of iconic memory, causing the visual trace to decay more rapidly
options.feedback: Incorrect. There is no established evidence that auditory noise directly shortens iconic memory duration; the issue is more likely attentional in nature.

options.text: Noise reduced the capacity of iconic memory, preventing all visual information from being stored
options.feedback: Incorrect. The question states that sensory memory capacity is unaffected; the explanation must involve a different mechanism.

options.text: Noise caused echoic memory to overwrite iconic memory, destroying the visual information
options.feedback: Incorrect. Iconic and echoic memory are separate stores for different sensory modalities; one does not overwrite the other.

toLevel5.stem: Some researchers have argued that sensory memory should not be considered a true 'memory store' because it is merely a passive sensory afterimage. Which evidence would best counter this argument?

options.text: Sensory memory serves as a functional buffer that enables attentional selection, which is a necessary step in the memory system
options.feedback: Correct. The functional role of sensory memory in holding information for attentional selection distinguishes it from a mere afterimage and supports its classification as a genuine component of the memory system.

options.text: Sensory memory has the same duration as short-term memory, confirming it is an active memory process
options.feedback: Incorrect. Sensory memory has a much shorter duration than short-term memory (seconds vs. up to 30 seconds), so this claim is factually incorrect.

options.text: Sensory memory requires conscious rehearsal to maintain information, proving it involves active processing
options.feedback: Incorrect. Sensory memory does not involve rehearsal; that is a characteristic of short-term memory.

options.text: Sensory memory stores information permanently if it is emotionally significant to the individual
options.feedback: Incorrect. Sensory memory does not store anything permanently regardless of emotional significance; its duration is always extremely brief.

toLevel5.stem: In Sperling's whole report condition, participants recalled about 4 of 12 letters. In the partial report condition with an immediate cue, they recalled about 3 of 4 letters from any row. What can be inferred about the relationship between sensory memory capacity and reporting limitations?

options.text: Sensory memory stored all 12 letters, but the time taken to report items in the whole report condition allowed the iconic trace to decay
options.feedback: Correct. The partial report success with any cued row shows all 12 letters were initially stored. The whole report limitation reflects decay during the reporting process, not a capacity limitation.

options.text: Sensory memory stored only 4 letters at a time and the partial report cue helped participants guess the remaining items
options.feedback: Incorrect. Participants could accurately recall items from any cued row, which would not be possible if only 4 items were stored; guessing would produce much lower accuracy.

options.text: The partial report advantage occurred because the cue extended the duration of sensory memory beyond its normal limit
options.feedback: Incorrect. The cue did not extend sensory memory duration; it simply directed attention to a subset of stored items before the trace decayed.

options.text: Both conditions show that sensory memory has a fixed capacity of exactly 4 items regardless of the reporting method
options.feedback: Incorrect. The partial report data show that more than 4 items were available in sensory memory; the 4-item limit in whole report reflects decay during recall, not capacity.

toLevel5.stem: A psychology student claims that echoic memory is more useful than iconic memory because it lasts longer. Which evaluation of this claim is most balanced?

options.text: The claim oversimplifies the comparison because each store is adapted to the processing demands of its respective sensory modality
options.feedback: Correct. Iconic memory's brief duration suits the rapid processing of visual scenes, while echoic memory's longer duration suits the sequential nature of auditory information. Each is adapted to its modality rather than one being more useful than the other.

options.text: The claim is entirely correct because longer duration always indicates greater functional importance in memory
options.feedback: Incorrect. Duration alone does not determine usefulness; iconic memory's brief duration is well-suited to rapid visual processing and serves an equally important function.

options.text: The claim is entirely incorrect because iconic memory is always more important than echoic memory
options.feedback: Incorrect. Neither store is universally more important; each serves the processing needs of its respective sensory modality.

options.text: The claim is correct because echoic memory has greater capacity than iconic memory in addition to its longer duration
options.feedback: Incorrect. Both iconic and echoic memory have unlimited capacity; they differ in duration but not in capacity.

toLevel5.stem: Sperling's partial report technique demonstrated that the {{blank:1}} of sensory memory exceeds what can be reported, because the iconic trace {{blank:2}} during the time it takes to recall all items.
The different durations of iconic and echoic memory suggest that each store is {{blank:1}} to the processing demands of its sensory {{blank:2}}.
